extracted.intended_audience: masters of vessels, pilots, and coastal navigators / nautical readers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical pilotage and coastal navigation guidance for entering harbours, channels, and passes (soundings, beacons, buoys, tidal observations, and landmark bearings) along the southern Australian coasts and entrances to Bass Strait. Includes procedural bearings, placement/maintenance of marks, and advice for safe passage in variable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep beacons painted white for visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Beacons were erected on the shore by the Beagle's crew, for guiding vessels through the channels; they, however, require to be kept white, in order to show well against the dark ground behind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beacons that contrast with their background improve visibility from seaward; regular maintenance (whitewashing) is recommended so marks remain effective aids to navigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eastern Channel leading marks (Shear and West Beacons)
rubrics_metrics.description: The leading marks for entering eastward of the Middle Ground, generally called the Eastern Channel, are the Shear and West Beacons. The Shear Beacon must be kept a little open to the left or eastward of the West Beacon, until you get abreast of the lighthouse; after which, both beacons should be kept in one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the specified relative alignment of the two beacons until the lighthouse is abeam, then bring them into one line to keep the correct track through the Eastern Channel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course change near Shear Beacon to avoid kelp (use Barrel Rock red beacon)
rubrics_metrics.description: When within two cables and a half of the Shear Beacon, the course should be changed in the direction of the Red Beacon on the Barrel Rock, the first on the eastern side, to avoid a patch of kelp, extending one cable and a half in an easterly direction from the Shear Beacon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the stated range from the Shear Beacon, alter course toward the Barrel Rock red beacon to clear the kelp patch; use the Red Beacon as a practical avoidance mark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Western Channel dimensions and leading marks
rubrics_metrics.description: The Western Channel is two cables wide, with a depth, in the shoalest part, of 10 fathoms; it is formed by the Middle Ground on the eastern side, and the Yellow Rock Reef on the western... The Shear Beacon and the flagstaff at George Town in a line lead over the outer extreme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Navigate the Western Channel using the Shear Beacon / George Town flagstaff line as an outer lead, noting the channel width (2 cables) and least depth (10 fathoms) and the position of Yellow Rock Reef and associated buoys.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of buoys and beacon combinations to lead through Western Channel
rubrics_metrics.description: The Barrel Rock red beacon, and the high and low white beacons, erected by the Beagle's crew on the shore over Lagoon Bay, kept in one, lead through the Western Channel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the Barrel Rock red beacon and the shore beacons are kept in line, that alignment indicates a safe track through the Western Channel; follow these visual alignments to avoid shoals and kelp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of buoy colours and markings
rubrics_metrics.description: Shoals marked with chequered buoys, may be passed on either side; a red or black buoy, signifies that the danger extends from the eastern shore; and a white one, that it extends from the western.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and apply local buoy semantics: chequered = pass either side; red/black = hazard projecting from east; white = hazard from west. Also note shore beacon symbols (V sideways, dagger) used within the entrance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking shoals and banks with beacons/buoys (shore symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: The shoals, on either side, within the entrance of the river, are marked with beacons. Those on the western shore, have a letter V sideways with a vertical bar on the top; and those on the eastern a dagger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and use shore-mounted beacon symbols (V sideways, dagger) in conjunction with buoys to determine which side a shoal extends from and to choose a safe passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hebe Reef passing guide (alignment of white spot and lighthouse)
rubrics_metrics.description: The guide for passing northward of it, is a white spot on the North-West extreme of Low Head in one with the lighthouse; the latter will then bear East 16 degrees South.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified alignment between a conspicuous white spot and the lighthouse (and its bearing) as the navigational guide to clear Hebe Reef when passing northward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and apply tidal observations (times, rise, stream durations/velocities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The result of 115 tidal observations, taken three miles within the entrance, gives 12 hours 06 minutes for the time of high-water on the full and change day. The rise of tide was irregular, the least being 4, and the greatest 10 feet. The tides flow 5 hours 50 minutes, and ebb 6 hours 25 minutes, with a velocity varying from two to five miles an hour, according as the river is confined or open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make extensive local tidal observations to determine high-water times, rise ranges, and durations of flood/ebb and stream velocities; plan navigation accounting for irregular rises and strong tidal streams (2–5 miles/hr in this area).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighthouse characteristics and use as a range/fix
rubrics_metrics.description: The position of the lighthouse on Low Head is... The light is elevated 140 feet above the sea-level, and may be seen, in clear weather, sixteen miles from the decks of small vessels, revolving once in fifty seconds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note lighthouse coordinates, elevation, visibility range, and periodicity; use these characteristics to identify the light and as a navigational fix or leading reference when aligning other marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place buoys on banks and spits to improve approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: The approach to this harbour would be vastly improved by a buoy placed at the end of the spit extending nearly across from Point Wilson on the north shore... Another buoy at the east extremity of the bank on the north side of the channel, which is very steep to, and one at the west end of the bank on the south side, would render the navigation free from difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install buoys at spit ends and bank extremities to mark hazards and steep-to banks; well-placed buoys reduce difficulty and risk in approaches and make channels more readily navigable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harbour anchorage suitability and wharf placement considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Corio Harbour is in fact the best anchorage in Port Phillip... There is deep water in the south-western part, close to the northern side of Geelong, where, by erecting wharfs, large ships might discharge alongside, an advantage which can never be obtained at Melbourne.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess harbours for depth, bars and shoals, and potential for wharf construction; prefer anchorages and quay sites where deep water close to shore allows large ships to discharge alongside.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow specified bearings/landmark sequence for South Channel entry
rubrics_metrics.description: After passing Point Nepean steer for Arthur's Seat, keeping Point Flinders open south of Lonsdale Point until the last cliffy projection is passed and bears South 1/4 West. Then steer half a point to the left of Arthur's Seat, shutting in Point Flinders with Point Nepean, and keeping Point Lonsdale a little open of the latter... Pass on the north side of the buoy and then haul up South-East until the water shoals to five fathoms...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the given sequence of visual bearings and landmark alignments step-by-step to transit the South Channel safely; adjust course as specified when particular bearings/marks come abeam or open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place and use buoys to mark five-fathom bars and channel entrances
rubrics_metrics.description: Returning to the ship we placed a buoy on the five-fathom bar at the eastern entrance of the South Channel, the bearings from which are Whale Head South 33 degrees West, and Arthur's Seat South 79 degrees East; Points Nepean and Lonsdale being a little open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark shallow bars (e.g., five-fathom bar) with buoys and note their bearings from local landmarks so pilots can identify the buoy and steer accordingly through the entrance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for strong local streams and their effects (danger to small craft)
rubrics_metrics.description: The outward stream between the heads sometimes attains a strength of nearly 7 knots, and when opposed to a southerly gale, causes a sea dangerous to small craft; these gales heap the water up in all parts of the bay... In the West Channel the flood and ebb-streams have a velocity of from 1 to 2 1/2 knots; but in the south it seldom exceeds two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know local maximum stream velocities and directions (they vary by channel and location); avoid or prepare for passages where strong opposing streams and winds can produce dangerous seas, especially for small vessels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use depth and seabed composition (soundings) to determine position in thick weather
rubrics_metrics.description: Masters of vessels should endeavour, if possible, to make the land in the neighbourhood of Cape Otway; but if the weather be thick they may know they are in the fairway of the Strait when they get into sixty fathoms, fine grey sand; in the same depth, with a rocky bottom, ships will be to the southward, and off the west side of King Island...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In poor visibility use the lead: soundings and bottom quality (e.g., 60 fathoms fine grey sand vs rocky bottom) provide critical positional information to distinguish whether you are on the fairway or off dangerous coasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lighthouse siting principle to minimize risk (Cape Otway vs Cape Wickham)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a light were erected on Cape Wickham, and a vessel running for it should be to the southward of her position, she would risk sharing the fate of the Cataraqui... Whereas, if the light were on Cape Otway, a ship to the southward of her position would have the Strait open to run through, and to the northward, would discover her error, by falling in with the land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Site major lights so that a vessel off her position is steered toward safer water or will more readily detect error; prefer sites that reduce the chance of bringing ships near hidden hazards (practical risk-minimizing criterion for lighthouse placement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry out and publish lines of soundings across straits and channels
rubrics_metrics.description: From Port Western we carried a line of soundings across the Strait to Circular Head, the greatest depth midway between being 40 fathoms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey and record systematic soundings along planned transit lines; publish these depths so mariners can use them to plan routes and avoid uncharted hazards.
